original_summary: Durak is a shedding card game with a 36-card deck. Players attack with cards that the defender must beat, using a higher card of the same suit or a trump; a defender who cannot beat an attack takes the cards, and the last player left holding cards is the loser. The reviewed version, Duel Durak, cut it to two players, 6-card hands with no draw pile, a randomly chosen trump, one attack card plus one rank-matching add per bout, and penalty points over 4 deals.

review.evidence: No simple policy is safe. Always TAKE keeps picking up cards and scores large penalties. Always leading the lowest or highest card can be exploited by a defender who keeps trumps back. Seats are balanced because the first attacker alternates by deal. Choices visibly change who empties their hand first.

With 6 cards, no draw pile and a random trump, the deal is often decided by the holding alone. A hand has no trump with probability C(27,6)/C(36,6), about 0.152. In roughly 40-50% of deals one hand must take whenever the right suit is led, whatever its owner does. Over only 4 deals, chance decides an estimated 60% or more of results.

There is real skill: reading voids from TAKEs, saving trumps and timing the add. When both sides play sensibly, though, the deal result is mostly fixed by trump count and suit shape, so improving one's play buys little.

Hands are hidden and 24 cards are unseen, so inference exists. But there is no event before play that signals anything, and the trump is random. What a player infers rarely changes what they can do with a bad hand.
Penalties are pure arithmetic on hand sizes at the end of each deal. The lower total wins, and equal totals are a draw. No judge is needed.

It is text-only, turn-based and fits within 40 rounds, 13 steps, 4 choice steps, 15 attributes and 3 hidden elements. However, the first round of each deal needs two independent random draws, the shuffle and a separate random trump, against a limit of 1 per round.

problems: P1 (platform): Each deal needs two random draws in one round, the shuffle and an independent random trump suit, against a limit of 1.
P2 (luck): A random trump with 6-card hands means a trumpless or void hand often cannot avoid taking. The holding decides most deals.

P3 (luck vs memory): The suggested duplicate fix, replaying deals with the hands swapped, does not work between the same two players. In the replay each player has already seen one hand and now holds the other, so both know both hands exactly. Hidden information vanishes, and the replay is played under different information than the original, so it is not a fair comparison.
P4 (reasoning): Nothing before play gives a signal to read. Inference is limited to occasional voids shown by TAKEs.
P5 (headroom): Only one attack card plus one add per bout, from small hands, leaves few meaningful decisions per deal, so strong players cannot pull far ahead of merely sensible ones.
P6 (sample size): Six cards over 4 deals gives too few decisions for skill to show.

changes.what: Trump is no longer random. It is chosen by cut-and-choose. At the start of each deal, the first attacker, after seeing their hand, offers two different suits. The defender, after seeing their hand, picks one of them as trump. The deal's only random draw is the shuffle.
changes.why: This leaves one random draw per round. It also stops the shuffle from deciding the trump: each player shapes the trump with their own hand, so a trumpless disaster becomes rare.
changes.fixes: P1 (platform): Each deal needs two random draws in one round, the shuffle and an independent random trump suit, against a limit of 1.

changes.what: Trump selection by offer and choice replaces random trump, and the offer and choice are announced publicly.
changes.why: The offer reveals which suits the proposer is strong in, and the choice reveals which of the two the chooser preferred. Each player must weigh offering their own strong suits, which helps them but tells the opponent their shape, against offering a decoy. The chooser must read the offer. Hand strength now depends partly on a reasoned decision rather than on the shuffle.
changes.fixes: P2 (luck): A random trump with 6-card hands means a trumpless or void hand often cannot avoid taking. The holding decides most deals.

changes.what: The duplicate replay is not adopted. Every deal is a fresh shuffle, and the attacker role alternates by deal.
changes.why: A replay between the same two players leaks both hands. Luck is reduced instead through the trump choice, bigger hands and multi-card attacks, while all hands stay genuinely hidden.
changes.fixes: P3 (luck vs memory): The suggested duplicate fix, replaying deals with the hands swapped, does not work between the same two players. In the replay each player has already seen one hand and now holds the other, so both know both hands exactly. Hidden information vanishes, and the replay is played under different information than the original, so it is not a fair comparison.

changes.what: The public offer and choice act as signals, combined with the public record of every attack, defence and TAKE.
changes.why: Players get a structured signal to reason from before play, and the record lets them count cards and infer the opponent's suit lengths.
changes.fixes: P4 (reasoning): Nothing before play gives a signal to read. Inference is limited to occasional voids shown by TAKEs.

changes.what: The attack may be 1, 2 or 3 cards of the same rank, which the defender must beat one by one or else take all. This replaces the separate ADD and second-defence steps, freeing two choice steps for the trump offer and choice.
changes.why: Durak's rank-matching pressure is kept, and attackers gain a richer decision: lead a pair to overload the defender, or hold it back. The choice-step budget stays at 4.
changes.fixes: P5 (headroom): Only one attack card plus one add per bout, from small hands, leaves few meaningful decisions per deal, so strong players cannot pull far ahead of merely sensible ones.

changes.what: Hands are 8 cards instead of 6, with 20 cards set aside, still with a 10-bout cap per deal and 4 deals.
changes.why: Larger hands lower the chance of a hopeless holding and add more decisions per deal. Multi-card attacks keep deals inside 10 bouts.
changes.fixes: P6 (sample size): Six cards over 4 deals gives too few decisions for skill to show.

keeps: The 36-card deck from 6 to Ace and the Durak beating rule: a higher card of the same suit, or any trump over a non-trump.

Attacker and defender roles. The defender beats every attack card or takes them. A successful defence discards the cards and the defender becomes the attacker. After a take, the same player attacks again.
Attacking with cards of matching rank to overload the defender.
Being left holding cards is what loses (the durak), scored as penalty points.
Two players, 4 deals, alternating first attacker, and a 10-bout cap per deal.

recommendation.reason: Durak's core is attack, beat-or-take and card counting, and it fits the limits. The fixes are a cut-and-choose trump that uses no extra random draw, multi-card rank attacks inside the choice budget, and larger hands to reduce the luck of the deal.

variation.name: Offered-Trump Duel Durak
variation.summary: A two-player Durak over 4 deals. Each deal, the first attacker offers two suits as possible trumps and the defender picks one. Players then attack with 1 to 3 cards of one rank, which must be beaten or taken. Cards left in hand become penalty points, and the lower total wins.
variation.rules:
CARDS. There are 36 cards: four suits (Clubs, Diamonds, Hearts, Spades), each with ranks 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, J (11), Q (12), K (13), A (14). Suit order, used only to break ties, is Clubs, Diamonds, Hearts, Spades.

BEATING. Once a trump suit is set, card X beats card Y if (a) X is the same suit as Y and of higher rank, or (b) X is a trump and Y is not. Nothing else beats.

STRUCTURE. The game has 4 deals. Each round is one bout. There are at most 10 bouts per deal and at most 40 rounds in total. Player 1 is the first attacker (the proposer) in deals 1 and 3. Player 2 is the first attacker in deals 2 and 4. The other player is the first defender (the chooser).

STARTING A DEAL (these steps happen only in the first bout of a deal, when the deal's bout counter is 0):
S1. DEAL. Shuffle all 36 cards once. Deal 8 cards face down to each player; only the owner sees their hand. The remaining 20 cards are set aside face down, unseen by both and unused this deal. This shuffle is the only random event.
S2. OFFER. The first attacker names two different suits. If the answer is not two different suits, the offer is Hearts and Spades. The offer is announced to both players.
S3. CHOICE. The first defender picks one of the two offered suits. That suit is the trump for the whole deal and is announced. If the answer is not one of the offered suits, the first suit offered becomes trump.

A BOUT (every round), in order:
1. ATTACK. The attacker places 1, 2 or 3 cards from their hand face up. All of them must be the same rank, and their number may not exceed the number of cards in the defender's hand. An illegal attack (a card not in hand, mixed ranks, or too many cards) is replaced by the attacker's single lowest-ranked card; ties go to the earliest suit in suit order. The attack is announced.
2. DEFENCE. The defender either says TAKE, or names one different card from their hand for each attack card, saying which attack card each one beats. Every pairing must be a legal beat. Any illegal or incomplete defence counts as TAKE.
3. RESOLVE. If the defence succeeded, all attack and defence cards are discarded face up, out of play, and the defender becomes the attacker for the next bout. If the defender took, the attack cards go into the defender's hand and the same player attacks again next bout. All cards played, the result, and both hand sizes are announced. Add 1 to the bout counter.

ENDING A DEAL. After RESOLVE, the deal ends if either player has no cards or the bout counter has reached 10. Penalties:
- If exactly one player has no cards, the other player (the durak) adds the number of cards in their hand to their penalty total.
- If both have no cards, nobody scores.
- If the deal ended at 10 bouts with both holding cards, the player with more cards adds the difference in hand sizes to their penalty total. Equal hands score nothing.

The next deal then starts with its bout counter at 0 and the first attacker set by the schedule above.

ENDING THE GAME. The game ends when deal 4 has ended. If round 40 finishes during a deal, that deal is scored as if it had reached its 10-bout cap.
variation.objective: When the game ends, the player with the lower total penalty wins. If the two totals are equal, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Luck of the deal shrinks because the trump is shaped by both players' choices rather than a coin. The proposer cannot simply offer their two strongest suits, because the chooser will pick whichever of those suits suits the chooser better. The chooser must also infer the proposer's shape from the offer, since every offered suit is a suit the proposer may well hold. In play, multi-card same-rank attacks create real tension: whether to spend a pair now, whether to beat cheaply or with a trump, and whether to take rather than burn trumps. The public record of the offer, choice, plays and takes supports card counting and void inference. Thoughtless policies can all lose: always-TAKE accumulates penalties; always-lowest-lead and always-first-suit choices are exploitable; a defender who burns trumps early is overloaded later. There is no talk, because the game is two-player and zero-sum.

balanced.evidence:
SEATS. P1 attacks first in deals 1 and 3, and P2 in deals 2 and 4. The setup is symmetric over the 4 deals, so neither seat gains from move order. Within a deal the first attacker does have an edge, because the defender carries the risk of failing to beat the last card. The alternation cancels this.

CORE ARITHMETIC. Every bout the attacker plays c cards (1 or 2).
- If the defender beats them all, both hands fall by c. The equal-size relation is kept.
- If the defender says TAKE, the defender grows by c plus the number of beaters played, and the attacker shrinks by c.
- With no TAKEs at all, the hands go 6/6, 5/5, ..., 0/0. Both empty together, so nobody scores.
- Penalties therefore arise only from TAKEs. The player who is forced to take more is penalised.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES, judged by the winner rule:
(a) Always TAKE. You never shed a card as defender, and the opponent sheds every bout. You are durak in essentially every deal and lose against sensible, random and most thoughtless opponents.
(b) Always attack with the first or lowest card, never add, and beat with the lowest legal beater. This is close to sensible baseline play. It is beaten by an opponent who leads into suits you have shown you cannot cover, and by one who adds matching ranks. It loses some games, so it does not 'never lose'.
(c) Always lead the highest card. This wastes aces and trumps that should be kept for defence. Sensible play exploits it, so it is not dominant.
(d) Always PASS at ADD. This gives up tempo. Adding a matching rank can force a TAKE, so PASS is not dominant either.
(e) Random play against sensible play. Random play makes illegal or wasteful defences and loses most deals.

DOMINANCE. Beating when you can is usually better than TAKE. However, TAKE can be right in order to save the only trump for a later lead, so no option is strictly dominant whatever the opponent does.

CONCLUSION. Both players can realistically win. There is no labelled payoff ordering to misdescribe.

playable.evidence:
WHAT IS SOUND.
- The rules cover every case: an illegal attack plays the lowest card, illegal defences count as TAKE, and ADD is skipped when either hand is empty.
- The deal end is checked after RESOLVE.
- 4 deals of at most 10 bouts each is at most 40 rounds, which matches the round cap.
- Scoring is pure arithmetic on hand counts. Nothing needs a judge, a board or a clock.
- It is a two-player game, so leaving out talk is correct.
- Hidden elements are 2 hands plus the 24 set-aside cards, which is 3 and within the limit.
- 13 steps, 4 choice steps and 15 attributes are all within limits.
- Setup can sit in flat steps guarded by `when bout_counter==0`.

THE VIOLATION. The first round of every deal needs TWO independent random draws: the 36-card shuffle and deal, and a separate uniform choice of the trump suit. The limit is random_draws_per_round at most 1. The designer's own claim of 1 draw per round understates what the rules require.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
NO TALON. Each deal is played out with only the 6 dealt cards and nothing is ever drawn. A deal is won by the player who takes less often, and the ability to avoid taking is set mostly by the holding.

HOW OFTEN THE HAND IS DECISIVE.
- P(a hand has no trump) = C(27,6)/C(36,6) = 296010/1947792, about 0.152.
- P(a hand is void in a given non-trump suit) is also about 0.152.
- So in roughly 40-50% of deals at least one player holds a hand that must take whenever the other leads the right suit.
- When the opponent holds 2 or more trumps against your 0, no defence choice prevents that.

WHEN BOTH PLAY WELL. Both lead the lowest card in a suit the opponent has shown weakness in, beat cheaply, keep trumps and add matching ranks. The deal outcome is then largely fixed by trump count and suit distribution.

TOO FEW SAMPLES. With only 4 deals, the sample is far too small for skill to average out.

WHERE SKILL ENTERS.
- Inferring voids from TAKEs.
- Choosing when to add.
- Saving trumps for later bouts.
These are real but secondary.

ESTIMATE. Chance decides about 60% or more of results. A stronger reasoner is not clearly favoured.

required_changes: Playable: use a single random draw per deal. Shuffle once, deal 6 cards to each player, and set trump to the suit of the 13th card of the shuffled deck (announce it face up), instead of a separate random trump choice.

Reasoning over luck: make it a duplicate game. Deals 3 and 4 replay the exact hands and trump of deals 1 and 2 with the hands swapped between players, and the first attacker of each pair also swapped. Stored hands use the attribute budget, which stays within 20. Only deals 1 and 2 need a random draw. This cancels the hand quality, so the winner is whoever played the same cards better.

Optionally, to strengthen inference: announce the number of trumps each player holds at the start of each deal, or let the defender also add matching ranks to a taken table. Either gives more to reason about without adding steps beyond the limit.

balanced.evidence: Main decision (defence) table, from the defender's view, when a legal beat of k attack cards exists. BEAT: defender sheds k cards, attacker sheds k cards, defender becomes attacker. Net hand difference unchanged, and the defender gains the initiative. TAKE: defender gains k cards, attacker sheds k cards and attacks again. Net difference swings by 2k against the defender. TAKE can be preferable only for keeping trumps for later, so it is a real trade-off rather than a free option. Attack options: 1, 2 or 3 same-rank cards. Each card attacked is a card shed whether it is beaten or taken. Multi-card attacks are limited by the defender's hand size and by holding pairs or trips, so no attack size is strictly best regardless of hands. Thoughtless policies under the winner rule (lower penalty wins): (1) Always TAKE: the defender gains every attack card and never gets the initiative. The opponent empties their hand and the TAKE player scores their whole hand (about 8 to 16) each deal, so it loses to sensible and to random play. (2) Always attack with the single lowest card, and beat whenever possible with the lowest beating card: it never uses rank groups, so it sheds 1 card per bout against up to 3. It typically loses the shedding race to sensible play, and it draws or wins only against random play. It is not undefeated. (3) Always attack with the maximum legal group: this spends pairs and trips at low value and leaves trumps unprotected. A sensible defender beats low groups with low same-suit cards. It can lose. (4) An illegal or empty answer defaults to TAKE or to the lowest card, both of which are weak. No policy never loses. Trump selection is a two-step offer and choice. The proposer knows their own 8 cards. The chooser picks the better of two suits for their own hand: expected trumps per hand is 8×9/36 = 2, and the chooser takes the maximum of two such counts. So the proposer must offer suits that are not worse for them, which is a real tension with no dominant offer. Seat edge: the first attacker in a deal sheds first (initiative), but the schedule gives each player 2 of the 4 deals as first attacker and the other 2 as chooser. Any move-order edge cancels over the game. Both players can win. Penalties are integers, so draws are possible but not structurally forced.

playable.evidence: The rules are complete. Beating is defined precisely. Attack legality is defined: same rank, 1 to 3 cards, no more than the defender's hand size. Illegal attacks default to the lowest card, with ties broken by suit order. An illegal or incomplete defence counts as TAKE. A bad offer defaults to Hearts and Spades. A bad choice defaults to the first offered suit. Resolution and the next attacker are specified for both outcomes. The deal ends after RESOLVE if a hand is empty, so the attacker always holds cards at ATTACK and the defender always holds at least 1 card. Penalties cover all three end cases. The game is finite: 4 deals of at most 10 bouts gives at most 40 rounds, and the round-40 clause can only coincide with bout 10 of deal 4, so it is consistent. The winner is lower total penalty, which is arithmetic on kept numbers. Limits: steps 16 of 20 are allowed. Choice steps: in a deal's first bout there are OFFER, CHOICE, ATTACK and DEFENCE, which is 4 of 4. Other bouts have 2. Attributes 16 of 20. Hidden elements are 2 hands plus the 20 set-aside cards, 3 of 3. Random draws are 1 shuffle per deal, at most 1 per round. Rounds 40 of 40. The deal-start steps are single steps gated by `when bout counter = 0`, which is allowed. It is not a conditional block. Hidden hands, sequential choice and fixed rounds are all supported. No board, judge or clock is needed. With 2 players, the absence of talk is appropriate. This is not a cooperative repeated game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance is the single 8-card deal per deal. The trump mechanism reduces hand-strength luck. The chooser picks the better of two suits for their own hand. The proposer must anticipate this, so a hand weak in raw trumps can still pick or steer a good trump. Over 4 deals with alternating roles, deal variance partly averages out. Rough estimate: chance decides about 30 to 40% of outcomes between equal players, and less when the players are unequal. Things to infer: (a) the offer reveals the proposer's view of their suits, and the chooser can read which suits the proposer avoided; (b) taken cards become known holdings of the opponent; (c) played and discarded cards narrow the opponent's 8 among the 28 cards the observer cannot see; (d) failures to beat reveal voids or low holdings. Ways to act on it: attack with groups in suits the opponent appears to lack, save trumps, choose between beating and taking, and pace the 10-bout cap. If both play well, the winner is not fixed by the deal: the trump choice, sequencing and conservation of trumps still swing results. A reasoning player clearly beats lowest-card or always-take play. The 20 set-aside cards limit perfect endgame counting, which keeps inference probabilistic but still present.
